one_liner: Header-only SwissTable-style hash map: 1.8-5.5x faster than std::unordered_map on 1M uint64 keys, but slower than phmap on lookups.
what_it_does: fastcpp::flat_hash_map<Key, T, Hash, KeyEqual> is an open-addressing hash map from the fastcpp library in the developer source repo. It replaces std::unordered_map when you can give up reference stability. The API uses std names for a subset of the interface: find/contains/count, emplace, insert(const value_type&), operator[], erase(key or iterator), reserve/rehash, clear, and forward iteration over pair<const Key, T>. Heterogeneous find(std::string_view) and find(const char*) work through the transparent default hasher and std::equal_to<>, but there is no allocator parameter, at(), try_emplace, insert_or_assign, initializer-list or range constructor, swap, or bucket interface.
how_it_is_fast: It is an independent implementation of Google's SwissTable design (absl::flat_hash_map). Entries live in one power-of-two slot array, so the index is a mask rather than a prime modulo, and a parallel array holds one control byte per slot: 7 bits of the hash, or an empty/deleted tag. A 16-slot group is filtered with one SSE2 compare+movemask, with an 8-lane SWAR fallback on other targets, so a hit is usually one control-byte load plus one key compare and a miss usually ends at the first group with an empty lane. Slots and control bytes share a single allocation instead of one node per entry. Keys are mixed with splitmix64 (integers, pointers) or a wyhash-style 64x64->128 multiply-fold (strings), because std::hash on integers is the identity in libstdc++ and libc++, which a masked table cannot use.
when_to_use: Large maps (well beyond cache) of integer or pointer keys where many lookups miss: on 1M uint64 keys, misses took 9.7 vs 44.7 ns (4.6x) and hits 18.9 vs 33.7 ns (1.78x) against libstdc++ std::unordered_map.

Build-heavy workloads where maps are filled and torn down often: 1M inserts after reserve() measured 34.7 vs 191.7 ns per insert (5.5x). This is the one path where it also edged the vendored phmap (1.07-1.10x).

String-keyed symbol or lookup tables holding std::string keys and probed with std::string_view or string literals: 2.18x on 200k all-hit lookups. On the repo's 92-keyword set it measured 8.86 vs 23.2 ns.
x86-64 builds: the 16-wide group match needs only SSE2, which is baseline on x86-64, so no -march flag is required.
When you want a Swiss table you can read end to end and vendor: one 535-line header, MIT, standard library only.
when_not_to_use: Lookup-dominated workloads: phmap::flat_hash_map, vendored in the same repo because of this result, is 1.29x faster on hits and 1.39x faster on misses (VENDORING.md recorded 1.21x/1.55x in another run). It is also far more mature.
Code that needs stable references or pointers to elements across inserts, or non-movable mapped types (e.g. std::mutex). Use std::unordered_map or a node-based map.

Small, cache-resident tables and non-x86 targets. In CI smoke runs, which the repo says are not reliable for timing, 1,000-key hit lookups on x86 roughly tied libstdc++ (3.6 vs 3.7-4.2 ns). On macOS arm64 (SWAR path, libc++), std::unordered_map was about 2x faster on 1,000-key lookups and roughly even on 1M-key hits. There is no NEON path.
Untrusted or adversarial keys: the default hashes are unseeded (fixed constants, and splitmix64 is an invertible bijection), so colliding keys can be precomputed.

Memory-tight or allocator-controlled code: there is no allocator hook, the table never shrinks on erase, and capacity rounds up to a power of two at a 7/8 maximum load. 1M uint64->uint64 entries used 35.7 bytes/entry in a table about 48% full.

integration.dependencies: none beyond the standard library, but the header includes 5 sibling fastcpp headers (core/bits.hpp, core/cpu.hpp, core/macros.hpp, hash/hash.hpp, hash/mix.hpp). The repo's fastcpp::fastcpp CMake target also links all ten vendored third-party libraries, so copying the six headers is lighter than add_subdirectory.
integration.min_toolchain: C++20 for this header (<bit> countr_zero/countl_zero, std::is_constant_evaluated); the benchmarks were built as -std=c++20. The repo itself now builds as C++23 and lists gcc 13+, clang 17+, MSVC 19.35+. CI covers gcc and clang on Linux and Apple clang on macOS; MSVC is not tested.
integration.platforms: x86-64 (SSE2 group match, no AVX needed); any other target, including aarch64, uses an 8-lane portable SWAR fallback that the header says is about half the speed on a miss. Container tests passed on a macOS arm64 CI runner.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. There is no internal locking; find/contains only read the table, but emplace, operator[], erase and rehash need external synchronization.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same value_type and core method names, but no allocator parameter, at(), try_emplace, insert_or_assign, initializer-list/range construction, swap or bucket API; erase(iterator) returns void; references are not stable; and the default hasher only covers integers, enums, pointers, std::string and std::string_view.

gotchas: Growth invalidates all references, pointers and iterators. emplace() and operator[] check the growth threshold before looking for the key, so m[k] on a key that already exists can still rehash the table.

rehash(n) doubles an undersized request only once, then reinserts with no capacity check. If size() exceeds twice max(16, next_pow2(n)), it never returns: for example rehash(0), the usual std::unordered_map shrink idiom, on any map with more than 32 entries. This comes from reading rehash/insert_unchecked; no test covers it.

Hash is default-constructed on every call (Hash{}(key)), so stateful or seeded hasher objects are not supported. It must return a well-mixed 64-bit value: the top 7 bits become the control tag and the low bits pick the group, so a 32-bit or identity hash degrades every probe. Floats, std::pair and user types need a custom Hash or the code does not compile.

erase(iterator) returns void, so the it = m.erase(it) loop idiom does not compile. Erased slots can stay tombstones until the next rehash, and iteration scans every control byte, so iterating a sparse or heavily-reserved table costs O(capacity).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: No siblings catalogued yet. Inside its own repo the rival is the vendored phmap::flat_hash_map, which wins lookups by 1.29-1.39x while this map wins only the reserve+insert build path by 1.07-1.10x; choose it for build-heavy use or when you want a small dependency-free header rather than a mature library.
verified_claims_summary: Against libstdc++ std::unordered_map (gcc 13.3.0, -O2 -march=native, minimum of 7 samples, on a 4-core Intel Xeon @ 2.10GHz shared cloud VM running Ubuntu 24.04), the author's own benchmarks measured 1M random uint64 keys: reserve(1M) plus 1M operator[] inserts, timed including teardown, at 34.7 vs 191.7 ns per insert (5.5x); hits at 18.9 vs 33.7 ns (1.78x); misses at 9.7 vs 44.7 ns (4.6x). 200k 'symbol_name_N' string-key hits measured 33.9 vs 73.9 ns (2.18x), with neither arm building a temporary string. These are first-party numbers from one machine, the repo says only within-row ratios are meaningful, and the same results file shows phmap beating this map on both lookup rows.
status_note: The repo (private:developer-source) is PRIVATE, so readers need access to see the code or benchmarks. It is young: the whole repo was written 2026-09-02..04, the header is unchanged since its first commit, there are no releases and 0 stars, and every CI run is red for reasons outside the map (an xsimd matmul bench build, a UBSan hit in string/parse.hpp), though the map's differential tests pass under ASan/UBSan. It is MIT-licensed and small enough to vendor as six headers.
